lead: Whether an SI engine knocks depends on the race between the flame and the end gas. Anything that makes the end gas hotter and denser shortens its ignition delay; anything that makes the flame slower or its path longer gives the end gas more time; and the fuel and mixture decide how quickly the end gas reacts at all. Textbooks group the factors in exactly these three ways: density (temperature and pressure) factors, time factors and composition factors. The same list explains the design and operating choices made to keep an engine knock-free.
prereq: You need: the race between the flame and the end gas (abnormal combustion).

sections.h3: Density factors: temperature and pressure of the end gas

blocks.text: A hotter, denser end gas reacts faster, so its ignition delay τ shrinks and knock becomes more likely.

items: Compression ratio: a higher ratio raises the temperature and pressure of the charge at the end of compression, so knock increases. This is the main limit on the compression ratio of a petrol engine.
Mass of charge inducted (load): a wider throttle, or supercharging, packs in more charge at higher pressure, so knock increases. Part throttle knocks less.
Inlet temperature: a hotter intake charge gives a hotter end gas, so knock increases. An intercooler on a turbocharged engine exists largely for this reason.
Temperature of the chamber walls: hot cylinder walls, a hot exhaust valve or a hot plug heat the end gas; poor cooling or a raised coolant temperature increases knock.
Spark timing: advancing the spark puts peak pressure nearer TDC, so the end gas reaches a higher pressure and temperature; knock increases. Retarding the spark is the quickest cure.
Power output: more power means more heat released per cycle and hotter metal, so knock increases.

sections.h3: Time factors: how long the end gas must wait

blocks.text: The end gas knocks if τ runs out before the flame arrives, so anything that shortens the flame's travel time reduces knock.

items: Turbulence: more turbulence (from squish, tumble and swirl) raises flame speed and reduces knock.

Engine speed: turbulence and flame speed rise with speed, so the burn takes less time; knock generally decreases as speed rises. Low speed and full throttle, such as climbing a ghat road in top gear, is the worst case.
Flame travel distance and plug position: a long path, as from a side-mounted plug, increases knock; a central plug or two plugs shorten it.
Engine size: a larger bore means a longer flame path and more time, so a large engine knocks more at the same speed; large petrol engines are therefore built with small cylinders, or many of them.
Combustion chamber shape: a compact chamber with squish keeps the end gas small, cool and close to the walls (see combustion chambers).
Octane number: a higher-octane fuel has a longer τ at the same temperature and pressure, so knock decreases.

Fuel–air ratio: knock is worst slightly rich of stoichiometric, at about φ = 1.1 (an air–fuel ratio near 13 : 1), where flame temperature and reaction rate are highest. Leaner mixtures (φ well below 1) release less heat and knock less; very rich mixtures also knock less, because the excess fuel absorbs heat as it evaporates.
Humidity: water vapour in the air acts as a diluent and lowers the flame temperature, so humid air reduces knock slightly.
Residual gas and EGR: exhaust gas left in or fed back dilutes the charge and slows the reactions, so it reduces knock, at the cost of a slower flame.

blocks.text: These factors act together. The worst case is a high-compression engine at low speed and full throttle, on hot intake air and hot coolant, with too much spark advance and a low-octane fuel. Modern engines stay near the knock limit by listening with a knock sensor and retarding the spark only when needed, so the driver gets most of the efficiency of a high compression ratio.

examples.question: For each change, say whether knock tendency increases or decreases and give the group and the reason: (a) compression ratio raised from 8 to 10; (b) spark advanced from 15° to 25° bTDC; (c) engine speed raised from 1500 to 3000 rev/min at the same load; (d) mixture changed from φ = 1.1 to φ = 0.85; (e) fuel changed from 91 to 95 RON.
steps: (a) Density factor. A higher compression ratio raises end-gas temperature and pressure, so τ shrinks: knock increases.
(b) Density factor. Advanced spark puts the burn nearer TDC, so peak pressure and end-gas temperature rise: knock increases.
(c) Time factor. More turbulence and faster flame, so the end gas waits less: knock decreases.
(d) Composition factor. φ = 0.85 is lean (85 % of the stoichiometric fuel–air ratio), well away from the worst mixture at φ ≈ 1.1: knock decreases.
(e) Composition factor. Higher octane lengthens τ: knock decreases.
examples.answer: (a) and (b) increase knock; (c), (d) and (e) decrease it.

examples.question: Intake charge at 330 K is compressed with n = 1.35. (a) Find the end-of-compression temperature for compression ratios 8 and 10, and for ratio 9 with a 350 K intake. (b) Find the air-standard Otto efficiency (γ = 1.4) for ratios 8 and 10. What does this say about the knock limit?
steps: Temperature after compression: T<sub>2</sub> = T<sub>1</sub> r<sup>n − 1</sup>.
r = 9 with 350 K intake: 9<sup>0.35</sup> = 2.158, so T<sub>2</sub> = 350 × 2.158 = 755 K, hotter than r = 10 on cool air.
Otto efficiency η = 1 − 1/r<sup>γ − 1</sup>: r = 8 gives 1 − 1/2.297 = 0.565; r = 10 gives 1 − 1/2.512 = 0.602.

Raising r from 8 to 10 gains 3.7 points of efficiency but heats the end gas by 56 K before any burning; a 20 K hotter intake at r = 9 heats the end gas by 43 K, more than the 27 K from raising r from 9 to 10.
examples.answer: (a) 683 K, 739 K and 755 K. (b) 56.5 % and 60.2 %. Compression ratio buys efficiency but costs knock margin, and hot intake air uses up that margin just as fast, which is why turbocharged engines need intercoolers.

traps: φ = 0.85 is a lean mixture, not rich: φ is the actual fuel–air ratio divided by the stoichiometric one.
Higher engine speed reduces knock (time factor); students often write the opposite.
Advancing the spark means firing earlier, more degrees bTDC; it increases knock. Retarding reduces it.
Knock is worst slightly rich (φ ≈ 1.1), not at the richest mixture; very rich mixtures knock less.
A larger bore increases knock through a longer flame path, even at the same compression ratio.

quiz.q: Name the three groups of factors that affect knock, with one example of each.
quiz.a: Density factors (compression ratio), time factors (turbulence or engine speed), composition factors (octane number or fuel–air ratio).

quiz.q: At which mixture strength is knock worst?
quiz.a: Slightly rich of stoichiometric, at about φ = 1.1.

quiz.q: Why does a higher engine speed reduce knock?
quiz.a: Turbulence and flame speed rise with speed, so the flame reaches the end gas in less time, before its ignition delay runs out.

quiz.q: Why does an intercooler let a turbocharged engine run more boost without knock?
quiz.a: It cools the compressed intake air, so the end gas starts cooler and its ignition delay is longer at the same pressure.

quiz.q: An engine on 330 K intake air has its compression ratio raised from 9 to 10 (n = 1.35). Find the rise in end-of-compression temperature.
An engine knocks. Suggest four changes, without changing the fuel, and say which group each belongs to.
quiz.a: Retard the spark (density), cool the intake or coolant (density), increase turbulence or squish (time), enrich slightly past φ = 1.1 or add EGR (composition).

quiz.q: Two engines have the same compression ratio; one has a bore of 70 mm and four cylinders, the other a bore of 100 mm and two cylinders. Which knocks first, and why?
quiz.a: The 100 mm bore engine: its flame path is longer, so at the same flame speed the end gas waits longer and is more likely to autoignite.

quiz.q: A car knocks on a hot afternoon climbing a hill in top gear but not on the flat. Explain using the three groups.
quiz.a: Low speed (less turbulence, time factor), full throttle (more charge, density factor) and hot intake air (density factor) together shorten the end-gas delay; changing down raises speed and lowers load.

beyond: Direct injection cools the charge as the fuel evaporates and lets compression ratios rise; variable valve timing lowers the effective compression ratio when knock threatens. Researchers rank fuels by octane sensitivity because downsized, boosted engines run in conditions beyond both the RON and MON tests. Search for knock-limited spark advance, octane index and charge cooling.

spec.aria: Three columns. Density factors: compression ratio, load, inlet temperature, wall temperature and spark advance all increase knock. Time factors: turbulence, engine speed, a central plug and a compact chamber decrease knock; a longer flame path or bigger bore increases it. Composition factors: octane number, a lean mixture, humidity and EGR decrease knock; a mixture near equivalence ratio 1.1 is the worst.
